name: Dive watch

card.summary: A water-resistant sports watch with a rotating bezel, worn as an everyday accessory to add a rugged, put-together look at the wrist.
card.note: Water-resistance ratings and ISO 6425 certification vary by model.

quick.overview:
A dive watch is a watch built for underwater use, with water resistance of at least 100 m, a rotating bezel for timing, and luminous markers. Typical models are rated around 200 to 300 m.[1]

People wear them as everyday sports-style watches. The bold dial, sturdy case and bracelet or rubber strap add a masculine accessory to casual and smart-casual outfits, which is how the style serves a person's overall look.[1]
quick.how: Dive watches are worn daily on a steel bracelet, rubber, nylon or leather strap. Cases of stainless steel, titanium or ceramic and legible lume dials are standard features.[1] Well-known examples include the Rolex Submariner, Blancpain Fifty Fathoms, Seiko models and Citizen Promaster.[1]
quick.risks: Water resistance depends on gaskets staying in good condition, and not every diver's watch is certified to the ISO 6425 standard because certification is voluntary.[1] Prices range widely from inexpensive quartz models to luxury mechanical pieces.

lead: A dive watch (diving watch or diver's watch) is a timepiece designed for underwater use, with water resistance of at least 1.1 MPa (100 m); typical models are rated about 200 to 300 m.[1] Its defining features are a rotating bezel for elapsed-time tracking, a gasketed water-tight case and luminous hands and markers.[1]

Dive computers have largely replaced these watches for active diving, but dive watches remain popular as backups and as everyday wear.[1] Many contemporary sports watches derive their design from the dive watch, and some owners regard them as jewellery or fine mechanical objects.[1]
In appearance terms, a dive watch is a style accessory. Its robust case and high-legibility dial are worn to complete an outfit and signal a sporty, practical aesthetic.

chain: Wear a sturdy, legible sports watch
Adds a bold, masculine accent at the wrist
Rounds out a casual or smart-casual outfit
angle.text: A dive watch is worn as an accessory that adds visual weight to the wrist and suits a wide range of outfits. People choose case size, dial colour and strap to match their wrist and wardrobe.

paras: The unidirectional rotating bezel turns only counterclockwise, so an accidental bump can only make elapsed time look longer, not shorter.[1] Water resistance is achieved with gaskets and sealant, and cases are made from 316L or 904L stainless steel, titanium or ceramic.[1] Non-toxic strontium-aluminate lume pigments such as Super-LumiNova keep dials readable in low light; older watches used tritium.[1]

The International Organization for Standardization introduced ISO 6425 in 1996. It requires a diving time indicator, readability in darkness, magnetic and shock resistance, corrosion resistance, strap strength and pressure testing at 125% of the rated depth. Conforming watches are marked "DIVER'S", but certification is voluntary.[1]

Rolex acquired the Oyster case patent in 1926, and Omega's rectangular Marine (1932) is credited as the first industrially produced diving watch for sale. Panerai supplied luminous Radiomir watches to the Italian Navy from 1936.[1] The Blancpain Fifty Fathoms appeared in the mid-1950s and was worn in Jacques Cousteau's film Le monde du silence, which won the 1956 Palme d'Or. The Rolex Submariner debuted in 1954 and is often called the first modern dive watch.[1]
Seiko's 62MAS (1965) was Japan's first professional diver's watch, and the Rolex Sea-Dweller (1967) and Omega Seamaster 600 PloProf (1970) pushed ratings to 600 m and beyond.[1]
